title: Singing the verses
hookLine: these poems were memorized and chanted for centuries before being written down
last: EACH KEPT IN ITS OWN TEMPER.

lines: IN THE MOUTH AND THE EAR.
cards: Before dawn, in the Buddha's dwelling, a teacher turns to a visiting monk and says, let the teaching come to you to speak.

And the monk begins to recite from memory, in a steady, intoned voice, a whole chapter of verses, start to finish, while the teacher listens. It's in the Udana, and in the Vinaya too. Nobody in the story opens a book.
Today, the elders' songs as they first lived: in the mouth and the ear.

teach.b: First, who's reciting. His name is Sona too, Sona Kutikanna, a different monk from the Sona with the bleeding feet. He has traveled a long way to see the Buddha, and they spend the night in the same dwelling.
At dawn, invited, he intones a chapter of verses from the Sutta Nipata.

When he finishes, the Buddha praises him: good, monk, you've learned these well, kept them well in mind, and you speak them clearly, with a fine voice. Memory and delivery, both. Second, where the line is.
The Vinaya tells of monks who chanted the teaching in a long, drawn-out singing voice, the way songs are sung for entertainment. People complained.
The Buddha forbids it and gives his reasons: the singer gets caught by the sound, the listeners do too, concentration breaks, and those who come later copy the style.
Yet he allows intoning, a steady chant that carries the words. The voice serves the verse, not the other way around. Third, how long the voice carried them.
The chronicle of Sri Lanka, the Mahavamsa, says that monks in earlier times passed down the texts and their commentary by mouth.
Then, seeing that people were declining, they came together and wrote them down in books, so the teaching would last. Tradition holds that the elders' songs traveled that same road.
Fourth, what that road asks of a voice: memory, clear speech, attention on the words. In this telling, the page came late.
The verses were sung before they were written, and wherever they're chanted now, a voice still carries them.

how: In Theravada monasteries, texts are memorized in Pali and chanted in a steady intoned style, the kind of chant the Vinaya allows.

o: a drawn-out song sung to entertain
a written copy of the verses on palm leaves
a steady chant for reciting the teaching

games.q: how the verses traveled: tap the pairs.
p: recited a chapter of verses at dawn
says monks later wrote the texts down

s: the elders wrote their songs on palm leaves as they composed them
tradition says the texts were passed down by mouth and written down later.
the Buddha praised a monk for reciting verses well from memory
he praised Sona Kutikanna's memory and his clear, fine delivery.
the Vinaya allows chanting the teaching in any singing style
it forbids a long, drawn-out singing voice and allows a steady intoning.

games.q: you're the Buddha. monks have started chanting the teaching in a long, drawn-out singing voice, like entertainers. what do you do?
o: let them: the more beautiful the better.
forbid the singing style, but allow a steady intoning.
games.why: in the Vinaya he forbids the drawn-out singing voice, giving his reasons, and allows intoning, a chant that carries the words.

practice: Choose something short you already know, or Subhuti's lines: my hut is roofed and snug, so rain if you like.

Sit up a little and say them quietly in an even voice, not performing, just carrying them, then once more, a little slower. Notice where your memory slips and where it holds, and let the words come and go with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Sarabhanna. The steady chant allowed for reciting the teaching: how the elders' songs lived first in the voice, memorized and passed mouth to ear, long before anyone wrote them down. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali sarabhanna: intoning, the steady chant the Vinaya allows for reciting the teaching.

carryVoice: Your line: sung before written. Memory and a steady voice kept these songs alive. See you tomorrow.
